title: Stone forms from Guerrero

objects.title: Architectural Model
objects.observed: The museum shows a serpentine form with uprights and openings.
objects.limit: The museum leaves the kind of building open.
objects.alt: uprights and openings in a small stone object

objects.title: Fish Pendant
objects.observed: The fish outline has a pointed head and tail. The museum records serpentine for this pendant.
objects.limit: The record leaves its particular wearer and occasion open.
objects.alt: a green stone outline of a fish

marketReply: I wanted a date beside the gate drawing. I can now show visitors the bracket beside each shape, with both numbers.
dockReply: I can carry the fish picture without saying the two pieces came from the same workshop.

title: Images on two Maya vessels

objects.title: Painted Vase with Ruler and Scribe
objects.origin: Maya, northern Petén, Guatemala, or southern Campeche, Mexico
objects.observed: The painted vessel shows kneeling figures and a seated figure. The record gives alternatives for its place of origin.
objects.limit: The pictured scene alone does not give an exact year for making the vase.
objects.alt: kneeling figures beside a seated figure painted on pottery

objects.title: Carved Vessel
objects.observed: The museum identifies a firefly motif carved on both sides of this vessel.
objects.limit: The image on one side alone cannot date the vessel to a specific night or event.
objects.alt: a carved motif on the wall of an earthenware vessel

marketReply: Now I can lay the painted scene and the firefly card next to each other. I’ll leave the long tail on the carved one.
dockReply: I’ll take the firefly card with its own wider dates. I can ask for the painted companion by its number.

title: Two garment records

objects.title: Saltillo Sarape
objects.material: Wool, cotton; tapestry weave, macramé fringe
objects.observed: The museum identifies tapestry weave and a knotted fringe in this Saltillo sarape.
objects.limit: The museum’s approximate date belongs to the garment. It does not date the beginning of the technique.
objects.alt: a long woven panel with narrow stripes and fringe

objects.title: Huipil
objects.origin: Guatemala, Quetzaltenango, late 19th or early 20th century
objects.material: Woven wool and embroidered wool and silk on cotton
objects.observed: The museum describes woven wool and wool-and-silk embroidery on cotton in this huipil.
objects.limit: The broad date covers the garment itself. Its separate material names do not identify its maker.
objects.alt: a woven garment with bands of embroidery

marketReply: I’ll put the two dated panels beside the bench. The date lines can stay apart; our examples of weaving can still sit together.
dockReply: I can carry one cloth example with the date still marked as approximate. I’ll keep the number for its neighbour on the back.

title: Cloth and paper in two collections views

objects.title: Lace Handkerchief
objects.observed: The 1889 Cuban handkerchief is recorded as plain-weave piña with silk embroidery.
objects.limit: The photograph of the handkerchief does not identify its intended owner.
objects.alt: a square handkerchief showing open work at the edge

objects.title: May Day, Central Park
objects.origin: Central Park, New York, United States (subject)
objects.creator: Maurice Prendergast (American, born Newfoundland [now Canada], 1858–1924)
objects.observed: Maurice Prendergast made this 1901 work in watercolour over graphite. It shows figures around a maypole in Central Park.
objects.limit: The date is for the work on paper and gives no connection to the Cuban handkerchief.
objects.alt: a watercolour scene of figures with long ribbons

marketReply: I can now pin the cloth and the painting under two years. The two peg holes make it possible to show the order without guessing a link.
dockReply: This slip fits in my box. Its date goes with its own source number. Leave the other one marked on the back for next time.

title: Two photographs of falling water

objects.title: Falls of Niagara
objects.creator: Alexander Henderson (Canadian, 1831–1913)
objects.material: Albumen print from wet collodion negative
objects.observed: Alexander Henderson’s albumen photograph of the Falls of Niagara has a 19 by 24.2 cm image. The museum gives the decade.
objects.limit: The object record does not narrow the exposure to a year within that decade.
objects.alt: an albumen photograph of falling water with a rocky bank

objects.title: Bridal Veil, Yosemite
objects.creator: Carleton E. Watkins (American, 1829–1916)
objects.material: Albumen print from wet collodion negative
objects.observed: Carleton E. Watkins’s albumen photograph of Bridal Veil at Yosemite has a 40.1 by 52.4 cm image.
objects.limit: The photograph’s making date does not support a change in the amount of water between the two places.
objects.alt: a tall pale waterfall photographed across a wooded slope

marketReply: I can use the diagram to show which years the two ranges share, beside the two different image sizes and makers.
dockReply: I’ll take the Watkins dates with the photograph credit. Our port copy should keep Henderson’s decade attached to Henderson.

title: Two ancestral Pueblo jar records

objects.title: Water Jar (Olla)
objects.origin: Southwest, Ancestral Pueblo, Tularosa Black-on-White style
objects.observed: The black-on-white jar has turning lines and jagged forms. The museum gives a Tularosa-style attribution.
objects.limit: The museum leaves the meaning of those particular marks open.
objects.alt: dark spirals and jagged lines on a pale jar

objects.title: Jar
objects.origin: Native North America, Southwest, Ancestral Pueblo, Sikyatki style
objects.observed: The museum attributes the earthenware jar to the Sikyatki style. Its label lists ceramic and slip.
objects.limit: The style is a catalogue attribution. This record does not identify the maker of this jar.
objects.alt: an orange pottery jar with a decorated shoulder

marketReply: I’ll hang the exact two numbers side by side. I can show the space between the brackets without claiming the workshops never overlapped.
dockReply: I can tell the reader the number, this jar’s dates, and the attribution. The potter’s name remains a separate question.
